coverage.basis: At least three actual decisions; absence of a newly disproved plan premise requires independent review.

findings.fact: The plan includes an impossible diamond branch.
findings.explanation: South holds DA and DK, so East cannot overtake West’s DQ. The alternative branch incorrectly treats that impossible event as a reason to preserve DA.
quotes: If East cannot overtake West’s DQ, South’s DA wins; otherwise preserve DA to capture a later diamond.

findings.fact: Keeping the plan retains its impossible diamond condition.
findings.explanation: The selected DA correctly beats DQ, but the retained advice still allows East to overtake DQ despite South holding both DA and DK. East’s actual D4 also resolves the current trick against that branch.
quotes: If East cannot overtake West’s DQ, South’s DA wins; otherwise preserve DA to capture a later diamond.

findings.fact: CQ cannot win or cash separately under South’s CA.
findings.explanation: CA already heads the current trick and necessarily beats CQ. Playing CQ consumes a separate club winner; it cannot perform the stated role of continuing dummy’s club winners.
quotes: Use dummy’s CQ to continue the club winners, then reassess the opponents’ club holdings and entries.
Play CQ over West’s C3. It is a winner now, and cashing it establishes whether the clubs divide favorably while keeping C7 and C2 as low cards.

findings.fact: The plan relies on club honors that will no longer exist.
findings.explanation: CA and CQ were consumed together in the preceding trick. CK is the only remaining partnership club honor, so after the prescribed CK there are no remaining club honors to use.
quotes: Continue with CK to cash another club winner and observe the defenders’ discards. Then use remaining club honors and HA as needed, preserving the spade ace and DK for later tricks.

findings.fact: The retained unfinished route still calls for nonexistent club honors.
findings.explanation: C2 legally follows under the winning CK, but keeping the plan retains its instruction to use further club honors. CA and CQ have already been played, and CK is in the current trick; the remaining clubs are C8, C6, C4, C7 and C2.
quotes: Then use remaining club honors and HA as needed, preserving the spade ace and DK for later tricks.

findings.fact: The plan calls C8 a cashing play while the reason treats it as a forcing play.
findings.explanation: CJ remains outstanding and beats C8. Leading C8 can establish the remaining clubs, but the explicit instruction to cash it conflicts materially with the accompanying recognition that the small clubs are not winners.
quotes: Cash C8 next, then assess whether the remaining clubs are winners.
East’s CT and West’s C9 are now known, so don’t count on small clubs as winners; C8 is the best available club to force out another card.

findings.fact: The replacement plan revives South’s already-played DA.
findings.explanation: The authorized history records South playing DA on the opening trick. South now holds only DK in diamonds, so the stated two-honor control and instruction to preserve those honors rely on an unavailable card.
quotes: South has DA and DK; preserve those honors and reassess after the defense’s diamond continuation.
South’s DA and DK remain the main diamond control.
